source_excerpt:
Growth & Talent Advisor · 20+ Years in Communications, Talent & Emerging Markets · EMEA & APAC Specialist · Husband & Father
Half of everyone who moved to a job in MENA this year came from India. That comes from a brilliant post I saw by Sam Marchant , who worked with Crustdata (YC F24) to trace 11,735 people who left a job outside the region for one inside it between November 2025 and October 2026. If you haven't seen it, it's worth a look. I wanted to add my own take, because I think plenty of people will read it the wrong way. The numbers first. India sent 5,881 people. The UK sent 1,171, Pakistan 901 and the US 456. The UAE took 70% of everyone, and Dubai alone took 5,265, about three times what Saudi Arabia got. A lot of people still think the UAE lives and dies on what's happening in Europe. If the West sneezes, Dubai catches a cold. I have never bought that as I have always seen a strong and growing Asian influence. The people arriving come from all over, and by far the biggest share comes from South Asia. India always has been the engine of this region and always will be. Anyone who has lived here knows that, but it's good to see it in black and white. What is interesting is that 27% of the people coming from the UK and 26% from the US landed at director level or above and from India it's 6%, and from Pakistan 5%. So the read is that the Gulf gets its volume from South Asia and a lot of its senior hires from the West. Far fewer Westerners are coming and landing jobs, but the ones who do are coming in to senior roles. Saudi tells a different story. Pakistan is the one big source where Saudi beats the UAE, 498 to 241. Saudi's top two sources are India and Pakistan, well ahead of the UK at 130 and the US at 94 and a third of the French movers went to Morocco, not the Gulf. So here's what I'd take from it. If you're a business, don't build your hiring plan around one source market, and don't assume the GCC needs the same talent plan, because the data says they don't. If you're a senior person in Europe or the US, the narrow door is slightly open, but you're being brought in to lead, so the bar is high. One caveat. This only counts people who left a job abroad for one here. It doesn't count people already living in the region, so it tells you who's arriving, not who's here. If you're hiring across the Gulf and want to talk about where to find your next senior leader, message me and of course reach out to Sam or Crustdata for more info on the survey.
The Saudi split is the part I would watch. Pakistan being the one source where Saudi beats the UAE suggests the two markets recruit through quite different networks rather than fishing in the same pool, which matters for anyone hiring across both.
The succession point is the one that costs money Justin McGuire senior hires imported, mid-level talent never developed. In MENA region's programs we've seen the gap show up as delivery risk: the people who actually know how the region moves aren't in the room when decisions get made. Our advice: Build the internal pipeline before the external hire becomes urgent. #MENAPM
That matches what you see in Dubai crypto and gaming teams too, a lot of the ops and support layer is India and Pakistan, while marketing leadership still comes mostly from Europe. Curious if that split changes as the local talent pool matures
The diversification point is the practical takeaway, but the source split needs a second filter before it becomes a hiring plan. A move recorded on LinkedIn is not the same as a successful hire, and the director-level skew from the UK and US suggests a different funnel, not just a different geography. I would pair this with time-to-fill and retention by source country before shifting effort toward any one corridor, because volume alone can hide a much weaker downstream outcome.
This also highlights the downside of hiring heavily from specific nationalities. It can limit opportunities for locals, create nationality-based groups within organizations, and turn hiring into a mess. I’m a South Asian myself, but honestly, we often hire our own, undercut salaries, and shut others out, and on top of that we don't have a concept of work life balance. The job market is getting overcrowded, with some candidates willing to accept salaries well below market rates, even for junior positions despite having years of experience. This is also why Saudization matters. The goal should be a job market where Locals get a fair shot at opportunities in their own country
Justin, the gap between 6% director-level hires from India and 27% from the West is striking. Having led centralised underwriting and risk governance at institutional scale, South Asian talent routinely brings the exact operational rigor GCC institutions need. Do you see regional boards actively shifting this perception as regulatory and governance frameworks mature?
I have a view on what this data say, the biggest risk is in the "volume from South Asia, senior titles from the West" dynamic which is the succession planning. Organizations that rely solely on external Western hires for director-level roles miss the massive competitive advantage of developing and promoting the mid-level talent that actually understands how this region moves, given that they have invested a huge amount of time here. The next five years will force that shift, whether companies plan for it or not, let's see
Dr. Saeed Bashirian 1w Report this post The war hit the GCC job market hard, then it found its feet again, but more slowly than before. It started on February 28, 2026, when the US and Israel struck Iran’s military sites and leadership. Gulf countries were quickly pulled into the fallout. March was the worst month: GCC hiring fell 13%, wiping out the region's small 1% growth in Q1. Headhunters said 50 to 80 percent of senior roles got frozen while boards asked for new risk reviews. The World Bank cut its 2026 GCC growth forecast from 4.4% to 1.3%. A WEF survey in April found 88% of top economists expecting weak job growth across the Middle East and North Africa, a full reversal from January. The ceasefire came on April 8, and hiring jumped 13% that month, though Cooper Fitch called it catch-up demand, not real confidence returning. That caution showed in the next quarter: GCC hiring was still down 3% in Q2. Qatar took the biggest hit, down 6%, tied to its energy and shipping exposure. The UAE was down 4%, Kuwait down 4%, Bahrain down 2%. Oman was the bright spot, up 1%, since its ports don’t depend on the Strait of Hormuz. Tourism, travel, hospitality and events took the earliest, hardest hits. Airlines only hired to replace people who left. Construction stopped bringing in foreign workers. Some global banks and tech firms froze expansion plans in Dubai and Riyadh. Sales, marketing and software also went quiet. Defense, cybersecurity, risk, and compliance never slowed. Finance and investment grew in Q2, partly a bounce-back after a quiet Q1. Real estate stayed strong on projects already underway. HR hiring held up, driven by Emiratisation. Family-owned UAE businesses barely paused. AI and cyber kept growing, a trend already running before the war. At the senior level, where it matters most for you: Dubai had around 19,000 open roles early in the year, split 35% finance, 30% tech, 20% healthcare, 15% government. VP pay in Abu Dhabi sat around AED 100,000 a month, roughly $27,000. Saudi roles tied to the giga-projects paid close to a million. Senior jobs didn’t vanish; they just slowed, and boards take longer to say yes than they did before the February war started. The bigger picture, from the ILO: if oil stays 50% above its early-2026 level, Arab states could see working hours drop 1.3% in a quick calm-down, and over 10% if things worsen, twice as bad as COVID in 2020, even in the mild case. About 40% of regional jobs sit in the most exposed sectors: construction, manufacturing, transport, trade, hospitality. Migrant workers are taking the biggest hit, and remittances to South and Southeast Asia are already starting to shrink. What it means for you: commercial and sales hiring has genuinely slowed since February, and boards move slower on senior hires than a year ago. But finance, risk, compliance, cybersecurity, and big project-delivery roles never stopped moving, and VP-level pay hasn’t dropped where roles are still open. 9 Like Comment Share Copy LinkedIn Facebook X To view or add a comment, sign in

Shariq Ali 1w Report this post “Do you have anything in the UAE or Qatar?” I’ve lost count of how many times candidates have asked me this after I said: “Are you open to moving to Saudi Arabia?” And honestly, I understand why. Saudi Arabia has a conservative past. But the country is changing, and so are the opportunities. As a recruiter, I have two jobs. Find the right talent. And help people see opportunities they might be overlooking. Here’s how I look at it. If you want lifestyle, the UAE is hard to beat. Dubai offers an international environment, personal freedom and an established expat community. But if you look at your career, the equation changes. 1. Your savings matter more than your salary. A studio in Riyadh might cost SAR 2,000 to 2,500 in some areas. In Dubai, a comparable studio can cost AED 5,000 or more. Your salary might be similar. Your savings might not be. 2. The competition is different. In the UAE, you're competing with a deep pool of international talent. Some candidates are willing to take a pay cut just to get into the market. In Saudi Arabia, certain specialised roles can offer better opportunities, particularly for people with skills that are difficult to find locally. 3. The growth potential is different. The UAE has an established talent ecosystem. Saudi Arabia is investing heavily in technology, transformation and major projects. That creates opportunities to take on bigger responsibilities and build experience in a rapidly developing market. Of course, it depends on the role, employer and industry. And I understand why some people choose the UAE for its lifestyle and freedom. There is no right or wrong answer. But if I had to choose my next move? I'd choose Saudi Arabia to earn more, grow my career and maximise my savings. I'd choose the UAE for lifestyle and personal freedom. That's my perspective as a recruiter who speaks to candidates and employers across the GCC. Sometimes, the biggest career mistake isn't choosing the wrong country. It's rejecting an opportunity before understanding what it could offer you. Your turn: Saudi Arabia or UAE?
